title: The next data stack has no UI
notes: DRAFT DECK. 90 minutes. Timing: intro 0:00, the agent 0:06, the analytics job 0:18, level 1 local 0:26, level 2 MotherDuck 0:40, level 3 your tools 1:00, level 4 your agent 1:12, wrap 1:24. Every hands-on slide is a placeholder until its exercise is tested end to end. Guess slides: let the room answer, then press R to reveal.

title: Two questions, then four levels
notes: Click a box to jump, or click HANDS-ON to go straight to the exercise. Row one gives the vocabulary: what is in an agent, and what an agent has to do in analytics. Row two is the four levels of agentic analytics work, each with a hands-on. At each level one more part of the agent becomes yours: first a local agent on your laptop, then MotherDuck so anyone can query, then your own MCP server, then your own loop and model.

title: Text to SQL is solved
body: Knowing what your business means by “revenue” is not.
notes: Every model in the room writes valid SQL. The hard part is the definition: which rows count, which units, which days. That is what the next 85 minutes are about. Keep this under a minute.

title: 01 · What's an agent?
body: A model that picks the next step, acts through tools, and loops.
notes: 0:06. Twelve minutes, talk only. Shared vocabulary for the rest of the workshop. Every definition on these slides links to its source.

title: Five definitions. What do they share?
notes: Read two of them, then ask the room what they all share. R highlights it: the model decides, there are tools, and there is a loop toward a goal. Willison's one-liner is the one to remember. The older textbook definition (Russell and Norvig: perceives its environment and acts on it) is left out until we check the edition we quote. Quotes checked against the source pages on 2026-11-02.

title: The loop
notes: The animation plays one question through the loop, turn by turn. Click the ring to pause or resume. Turn 1: the window holds the system prompt, the tool list and the question. The model writes a tool call (list_tables). The harness runs it, the result goes back into the window. Turn 2: same loop, now with a query. Turn 3: the model has what it needs and replies in plain text. That reply has no tool call in it, so the harness has nothing to run and the loop ends. That is the only stop rule: no tool call, no next turn (plus a step cap in the harness). The model never touches the data, it only writes the next message. Anthropic describes the loop as gather context, take action, verify work, repeat. ReAct (Yao et al., 2022) is the research origin.
sourceLabel: CLAUDE AGENT SDK · GATHER, ACT, VERIFY

title: The parts of an agent
notes: OpenAI's guide names three core parts: model, tools, instructions. LangChain adds the frame: agent = model + harness, where the harness is every piece of code, configuration and execution logic that isn't the model. Read the diagram left to right: a human asks, the harness builds the context, the model picks a step, a tool acts on the environment. The bottom row is what a harness like Claude Code adds. Keep this slide in mind: each level greys out what is rented and lights up what becomes yours.

title: What the model sees on every turn
notes: The model is stateless. Each turn, the harness sends the whole window again: system prompt, tool definitions (every MCP tool adds its name, description and schema), memory files, skill descriptions, the conversation and every tool result so far. When it fills up, the harness summarizes old turns. This is why a 10,000-row result hurts: it stays in the window. It is also why DuckDB's agent mode matters. Hands-on later: /context in Claude Code shows the real split.

title: Five places to tell an agent something
notes: This answers 'what is a skill file vs a system prompt vs a guide'. System prompt: the app's own instructions, every turn. AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md: repo conventions, loaded at session start. Skill: a folder with SKILL.md (and optional scripts). Only the name and description sit in the window until the agent decides it needs the body: progressive disclosure. MCP server instructions: how to use the vendor's tools. Guide: what the data means, stored in MotherDuck. The first four live with one person, one repo or one app. The guide lives with the data, so every agent with access can read it. That is chapter 2.

title: The harness: everything around the loop
notes: Same model, different harness, different agent. Claude Code's harness gives permissions (allow, ask, deny), hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse...), a sandbox, memory files, automatic compaction and subagents. At level 4 you write a much smaller harness yourself: a tool list, a step cap and the loop, in about 60 lines of Python.

title: A hook: code that can say no
code:
# runs before every tool call, with the call as JSON on stdin
if is_cloud_delete(call) and not teardown_unlocked():
    print("Cloud deletes are locked. Ask the human.", file=sys.stderr)
    exit(2)      # 2 = block the call, and the model reads why
notes: Simplified from the guard hook in parked/duckoffee (tested). In Claude Code, a PreToolUse hook that exits with code 2 blocks the tool call and its stderr goes back to the model. The model cannot talk its way past it. This is a harness rule. Level 2 adds the strongest layer, the database.

title: Four levels. One more part becomes yours.
notes: This is the plan for the next hour. Level 1, Local: Claude Code or Codex with DuckDB and a skill, everything on your laptop. Level 2, Remote MCP: data and compute move to MotherDuck behind its remote MCP server, so anyone you share with can query. Level 3, Custom MCP: you own the tools, with your MCP server in front of MotherDuck's. Level 4, Custom agent: you own the loop and pick the model with your own key. Click a row to jump.

title: 02 · What's an agent for analytics?
body: Text to SQL is solved. So what's left?
notes: 0:18. Eight minutes. Ask the room: if every model writes valid SQL, what is left for an analytics agent to do? Take two or three answers, then the next slide breaks the job into six tasks. Then look at which UIs it removes.

title: Six tasks for an analytics agent
notes: Ask the room to shout a guess for each box before pressing R. Pipelines (ingest, transform, schedule): Flights, Python runs on MotherDuck, scheduled or on demand (free plan: on demand only). Data apps: Dives, interactive React apps over live data, saved in MotherDuck. Context: Guides (level 2). Storage: MotherDuck databases, fully managed DuckLake, and local DuckDB for the laptop part. Permissions and sandbox: per-agent Ducklings, service accounts, read-only tokens, shares with secure views (level 2); each Flight run also gets its own isolated runtime. Observability covers all five: Flight Explainer (the run viewer MCP app), query history, and traces we store ourselves (chapter 6).

title: Too many UIs?
section: 02 · THE ANALYTICS JOB · THE NEXT DATA STACK HAS NO UI
notes: This is the title of the workshop. Each layer of the modern data stack ships two UIs: one to build things (connectors, models, schedules, dashboards) and one to watch them run. Count the window icons: ten UIs for one metric. Ask: how many browser tabs do you open to ship one metric?

title: When an agent builds, which UIs survive?
notes: Let people guess before R. Building moves to chat: in data, describing the connector, the SQL, the schedule or the chart is enough, the agent writes it. Some domains still need a custom builder UI (video editing, visual design). Watching does not go away: people still need dashboards, a view of pipeline runs, and a view of what agents did.

title: Chat to build. MCP apps to watch.
notes: MotherDuck's MCP server ships MCP apps, UIs rendered inside the chat client: the Dive viewer (view_dive) and the Flight Explainer run viewer (view_flight_run, opened from run_flight, enabled for everyone in prod, per the server commit history, untested). For agent traces there is no dedicated app: we store traces in MotherDuck and look at them with a Dive (level 4). Demo: run a Flight from chat and watch it in the Flight Explainer, then open a Dive.

title: Level 1 · Local
body: DuckDB on your laptop, a managed agent, one skill file.
notes: 0:26. Fourteen minutes: 4 of talk, 10 of hands-on. Harness and model are rented (Claude Code, or opencode with the workshop key). You own one skill file and the data on your disk.

title: DuckDB 2.0 talks to agents
sourceLabel: DUCKDB.ORG · AGENT MODE IN THE CLI
notes: The 2.0 CLI detects when an agent runs it (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot, or AI_AGENT set) and switches output. Flags: -agent forces it on, -no-agent off, DUCKDB_AGENT_MODE also works. In DuckDB's TPC-H test the agent read 123.6k to 50.8k tokens of DuckDB output (59% less), all 132 runs correct, slightly more turns. The two tables on the slide are illustrative, not captured output. Why local matters for agents: in-process, free, fast, nothing leaves the laptop, so it is the safest sandbox for an agent to explore. Open question: do MotherDuck clients support DuckDB 2.0 by the workshop date?

title: A skill is procedure. A guide is meaning.
code:
---
name: company-analytics
description: Answer business questions on the duckgen dataset with DuckDB.
---

# Company analytics

1. Read the tables with the DuckDB CLI before writing SQL.
2. Keep money in cents until the final SELECT.
3. Show the SQL you ran under every answer.
4. Build dashboards as one local HTML file.
notes: A skill tells the agent how to work. It is a folder with SKILL.md and optional scripts, loaded only when relevant, so it costs almost nothing in the window until used. At level 2 we add one line: call get_query_guide first. That line is where procedure (skill) meets meaning (guide).

title: Your data, locally
notes: Reference for the hands-on. Tested: this path reads. Each participant swaps in the S3 prefix of the company they drew. The café S tier: 1,764 shops, 7.7M rows in item_daily, 2024-10-07 to 2026-10-06.

title: Hands-on 1: a local analytics agent
steps: Save the skill file in your project.
Ask the agent to load your company’s Parquet from S3 into a local DuckDB file.
Ask for one clean table that answers your question.
Ask your question. Note the number and the SQL.
Ask for a dashboard: one HTML file you open locally.
doneWhen: dashboard.html opens on your laptop and shows your answer.
needs: Claude Code (workshop key via OpenRouter works)
notes: Tested 2026-11-02 on Gloamwick Studios (gaming) with Claude Code routed through OpenRouter (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, Sonnet 5.5): 16 turns, 3.4 min, $0.38. It loaded 8 tables from S3 into company.duckdb, found the boss rework (Android D7 14.5% to 10.7%, iOS flat) and the chest video (ARPDAU +17%), and wrote a working dashboard.html. The answer key agrees on the boss rework finding. DuckDB 2.0 Python loads the 5 main tables in about 5 s. Optional for fast people: /context and /mcp. At the end ask: who else can open your dashboard? Nobody.

title: To share it, you build all of this
notes: Inspired by the self-hosting DuckDB talk. A local agent is fine for you. The moment a teammate, a shop manager or another agent needs the answer, someone has to run storage, compute that isolates users, identity, access rules, context, pipelines, app hosting and observability. Pause on this slide.

title: Level 2 · Remote MCP
body: Same agent, remote compute and dashboards. Now anyone can query.
notes: 0:40. Twenty minutes: the longest level. Context, data apps, pipelines and access all show up here, because sharing is what makes them necessary.

title: MotherDuck runs these boxes
notes: Same boxes, run for you. Clients on the left reach MotherDuck through MCP or SQL. In the middle, the parts this workshop uses: identity and access (service accounts, tokens, shares, secure views), Ducklings (compute per user and per agent), Guides, Flights, Dives, and storage with DuckLake. On the right, what MotherDuck reads from: object storage, databases, DuckLake on your own bucket.

title: MCP: tools written once, for any agent
notes: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for a server to expose tools (and resources and prompts) to any client. The client lists the tools, puts their definitions in the context, and calls them when the model asks. MotherDuck runs a remote MCP server at api.motherduck.com/mcp: the same tools work in Claude Code, claude.ai, ChatGPT, Cursor or your own app. Tool names on the slide are from the production server. The server also sends instructions at connect time, with client-specific guides (the repo has separate dive guides for Claude Code, claude.ai, ChatGPT and other clients).

title: Same question. How many answers?
body: Post your number. Then we compare.
notes: Collect numbers in a shared sheet or the chat. Expect a spread. The traps are in the data: money is integer USD cents, Sunday rows exist with zero activity, pilot customer-days include zero visits, pilot visits are a separate sample and must not be added to shop revenue. The answer keys from duckgen give the right numbers. TODO: run the four questions with a bare agent before the workshop to confirm the spread is real.

title: How a guide reaches the agent
notes: Read from mcp-server on origin/main. Nothing is injected into the agent's context. The agent has to ask, and the server points it there in four places: get_query_guide (its description says to call it before writing SQL), the query tool's description, list_tables and search_catalog (they return relatedGuides), and get_flight_guide / get_dive_guide (guides under the reserved flights and dives topics). Guides are SQL underneath (MD_CREATE_GUIDE, MD_LIST_GUIDES), so a custom app can load them into its system prompt instead. A guide under the flights topic is procedure: that answers 'can a guide be a harness?' for ingestion.

title: Hands-on: write the guide
body: Then start a fresh session and ask the same question.
code:
# Juniper Counter: how we count

- Money columns are integer USD cents. Divide by 100.
- Shops are closed on Sundays. Sunday rows exist with zero activity.
- The loyalty pilot is a separate sample. Never add pilot visits to shop revenue.
- Pilot customer-days include zero visits. Keep them when averaging.
- Contribution excludes rent and salaried labor.
notes: Draft content taken from the duckgen spec notes. Check every line against answer-keys.json before the workshop. Participants ask their agent to create it with create_guide, attached to the café database so list_tables surfaces it. Do not use duckgen's guide.md as is: it contains the answer SQL and the planted stories. Grade the second answer against the answer keys. Look at the trace: did the agent call get_query_guide?

title: One Duckling per agent
notes: Hypertenancy: every user, service account or agent gets its own Duckling. At level 4 the agent you ship gets its own service account, so it gets its own Duckling too. Clean cost attribution per agent, and revoking one token stops one agent. Read scaling serves many end users through one service account with read-only Ducklings. Demo: an agent hammers heavy queries on its own account while a dashboard on another account keeps its speed. TODO: script the demo.

title: What stops teams from shipping AI on data
notes: Ask the room first: what would stop you from giving an agent access to your warehouse? Then map each fear to a control. Masking also limits what reaches the model provider: if the agent only sees masked values, that is all that can leave in a prompt.

title: Where to put a rule
notes: Four places, weakest to strongest. The message of the whole workshop: guides for correctness, the database for safety. People who hesitate want to hear that the fence does not depend on the model behaving.

title: Shop managers see their shop
notes: Draft, not run yet. Row filter by shop, cost columns left out (hidden columns do not exist for the consumer: SELECT food_cost_cents fails as missing). Service accounts have no email, so agents are matched with current_user. Secure views need Business or Enterprise (trials count): we run this in the devrel org and participants only query the share. Managing secure views with SQL needs DuckDB 1.5.6+, consumers need 1.5.5+ for every query shape. EXPLAIN hides the filter and copies of the share stay filtered.

title: Hands-on 2: move it to MotherDuck
steps: Add the MotherDuck remote MCP server to your agent.
Attach your company’s share and ask your question again.
Write a guide with create_guide. Start a fresh session and ask again.
Save your dashboard as a Dive and send the link to your neighbor.
Stretch: turn the load step into a Flight and open the run in the Flight Explainer.
doneWhen: your neighbor opens your Dive, and you can say whether the guide changed your number.

It attached the share, answered, wrote a private guide with create_guide and saved a Dive. The Flight stretch is not tested yet. Collect numbers before and after the guide for the spread slide.

title: Level 3 · Custom MCP
body: Your own MCP server, in front of MotherDuck’s.
notes: 1:00. Twelve minutes. Same managed agent. Now you decide which tools it gets, what they are called, and what is logged. This is how a product ships MotherDuck to its own users.

title: Own the tool surface
notes: From the MotherDuck white-label guide. Your server proxies the remote MCP server over streamable HTTP with a bearer token. It forwards a small set (query, list_tables, list_columns, search_catalog, the guide read tools), drops query_rw and Flight tools, and rewrites names, descriptions and instructions. One service account per tenant, read scaling tokens for read-only. A required question parameter is logged with tenant, SQL and outcome: that is your trace. The doc's example uses FastMCP 4.0.3.

title: Hands-on 3: your own MCP server
steps: Run the starter: uv run server.py. It forwards query, list_tables, list_columns and the guide tools under your names.
Rewrite the tool descriptions for your company.
Add one domain tool that wraps the SQL for your question.
Make question a required argument and log it.
Point your agent at your server instead of MotherDuck’s.
doneWhen: your agent answers your question with your tools only, and the log shows the question.
notes: Tested 2026-11-02 with exercises/3-custom-mcp/server.py (FastMCP 4.0.3, the version in the white-label doc): 5 turns, 28 s, $0.07, against 16 to 18 turns at levels 1 and 2, because the domain tool carries the SQL. Every question landed in questions.jsonl. Lesson from the first run: forward get_guide too, or the agent sees guide titles and cannot read them. The token stays in the server, never in the agent's context.

title: Level 4 · Custom agent
body: Your loop, your model, your link.
notes: 1:12. Twelve minutes. The last rented parts were the harness and the model. Here you own both: the loop is 40 lines, the model is any model behind the workshop key.

title: The whole agent, really
code:
messages = [system, question]
loop step in range(MAX_STEPS):
    reply = model(messages, tools)        # any OpenRouter model
    messages += [reply]
    if not reply.tool_calls:
        return reply.content
    for call in reply.tool_calls:
        result = mcp.call_tool(call.name, call.args)   # your MCP server
        messages += [tool_result(call.id, result)]
notes: Press H to walk the lines. This is the core of exercises/4-custom-agent/agent.py, tested 2026-11-02 with Gemini 3.8 Flash. Everything else in the file is plumbing: turn MCP tools into the model's tool format, start the server with the token, cap the steps. Notice what is not here: no permissions, no hooks, no memory. That is the harness you now own.

title: Build your agent
notes: The generator is one hosted app (built from /try patterns). Each knob is one component of an analytics agent. Next to the editor: a preview chat with a trace panel that shows every turn of the loop. Test the three context modes on the same question and compare against the answer keys. Then deploy: the agent gets a unique link. Nothing to install, nothing to deploy on their side.

title: Hands-on: break your neighbor’s agent
notes: Everyone gets two links. Agent A has the rule in its system prompt. Agent B runs as a shop manager through the secure view. Try to get other shops' numbers or the cost columns out of each. A is likely to leak, B cannot. Then fix your own agent with the harness and identity knobs. Collect the best attacks for the wrap.

title: Every agent, one table
notes: The Flight Explainer covers pipeline runs. For the agents, the generator writes every turn to a MotherDuck table (the way duckgen and /try write to llm_obs), and a Dive shows the whole room: steps per question, who called get_query_guide, who matched the answer key, which attacks got through. The answer keys are the evals.

title: Hands-on 4: ship your agent
steps: Open the generator and paste the workshop key once.
Pick a model, your tools, the step cap and who the agent runs as.
Test in the preview, then deploy and get your link.
Red team your neighbor: get another shop’s numbers or the cost columns out.
Open the Dive over the whole room’s traces.
doneWhen: you have a link anyone can use, and you know whether your neighbor broke it.
notes: The loop itself is tested: exercises/4-custom-agent/agent.py, 60 lines, Gemini 3.8 Flash via OpenRouter, tools from the level 3 server, 5 steps. It read the guide written at level 2 and returned the same numbers as the Claude run. The generator around it is not built yet. Key stored encrypted on the server, never in the URL or the browser. Links expire after 7 days and keys are revoked after the workshop.

title: One question, four levels
notes: Measured on 2026-11-02, one run each, same question on Gloamwick Studios: which live-ops changes moved retention and ARPDAU? Levels 1 to 3 ran Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5 through OpenRouter, level 4 our own loop with Gemini 3.8 Flash. The domain tool at level 3 cut the turns and the cost by a factor of 3 to 5. The guide written at level 2 made the level 4 run, on another model, return the same numbers. One run each, so treat these as an illustration, not a benchmark.
